Quantive to run their endpoint tests on staging and share results by 2025-09-22
Schedule canary run for the 2pm Pacific slot next Friday (2025-09-26)
Redwood to propose dedicated pool sizing options and cost delta by 2025-09-21
action_items: Liam Patel - export per-model p95/p99 latencies and throughput CSV - 2025-09-19
Tom Reeves - provide test harness URLs and sample payload sizes used in baseline - 2025-09-18

summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark results comparing Redwood hosted inference against the customer's baseline provider. Redwood presented updated p50/p95/p99 latencies and throughput after enabling KV caching and batch size tuning. Quantive raised questions about cold start variance, tail latency, and the cost tradeoffs for Dedicated vs hosted. Agreed next steps include sharing raw logs, scheduling a canary, and sizing proposals.
topics: cost vs latency for dedicated pools
next steps for canary and security docs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-17 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~55m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Liam Patel (Redwood); Sara Gomez, Tom Reeves, Priya Nair (Quantive)
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, hopefully you all got the agenda. quick call today to go over the benchmark numbers we ran against your baseline provider and walk through tuning we did this week
[00:28] Sara Gomez: yeah thanks Maya, quick note, we had a couple last-minute infra changes but should be fine, want to focus mostly on tail latency since that's been our blocker for UX
[01:05] Liam Patel: cool, i'll start with the numbers slide, apologies if some names are a bit off in the deck, auto-transcript did some funny swaps - but numbers are solid. baseline provider p50/p95/p99 for the 13B model at your payload distribution was 80ms / 420ms / 980ms, throughput ~320 tokens/s under 8 concurrent clients
[01:46] Liam Patel: on Redwood hosted with default batching we saw 60ms / 210ms / 480ms and throughput 410 tokens/s. after turning on KV prefix cache and tuning batch window to 30ms we got p95 down to 150ms and p99 to ~420ms; throughput jumped to ~520 tokens/s
[02:20] Tom Reeves: wait, the p99 number looks similar to baseline after tuning, is that because of cold starts or large generation tails?
[02:52] Liam Patel: good question, we dug into the raw traces - most of the p99 are warm requests with very long generation steps (rare >512 tokens) and a small number of cache misses that hit the full attention path. cold starts were a small fraction, maybe 3-4% of requests in our sample since this is hosted and we have autoscale spin-up
[03:28] Priya Nair: any idea why your p95 improved so much versus baseline but p99 didn't move as much?
[03:47] Maya Chen: two reasons - first, caching reduces repeated prefix compute which helps the mid-tail a lot. second, baseline provider seems to have higher variability on inter-request queuing under bursty concurrency, and their kernel scheduling on the instance type they used amplifies the tail. for p99 we recommended batching/quantization/and possibly dedicated pools to reduce variance
[04:15] Sara Gomez: can you quantify cost differences if we go dedicated? our procurement is sensitive to a 20% delta
[04:33] Liam Patel: quick ballpark: dedicated pool for your target throughput (500-600 tokens/s sustained) would be X GPUs (we'll send exact numbers) - estimate a 10-25% unit-cost increase vs hosted but you pick up predictability and lower p99 in our tests. the tradeoff depends on utilization and burst patterns
[05:02] Tom Reeves: you mentioned quantization earlier - did you try 4-bit per-channel and what's the quality delta?
[05:20] Liam Patel: yes we ran int4 and q4f16 variants, for your eval prompts we saw negligible quality regression (within edit distance threshold) for q4f16; q4_0 had a slight bump in rarer safety tokens - we flagged that. we'll share the eval spreadsheet. quantization reduced p50/p95 by ~10-15% and throughput increased ~20%
[06:00] Sara Gomez: about that eval spreadsheet, please include prompt sets A/B + scoring rubric, that will help our ML team validate quality tradeoffs
[06:28] Maya Chen: absolutely, Liam will attach that with the raw latency CSVs
[07:00] Liam Patel: on testing methodology - we used your supplied harness (thanks Tom) hitting 8 concurrent clients, payload distribution matching training set - durations are 20m steady-state windows, we excluded the first 2 minutes for warm-up. raw logs include per-request kernel times, queue time, decode time
[07:40] Tom Reeves: just confirming - is the queue time visible to us in the logs? sometimes baseline provider obfuscates that metric
[08:02] Liam Patel: yes it's there, we included queue_time and model_time columns in the CSV; queue_time is what contributed to that big variance for baseline
[08:28] Priya Nair: curious about region/residency: the baseline tests were in us-central1, can you run a quick sanity in eu-west-1 to compare?
[08:48] Maya Chen: we can, but that'll add a day; we'll prioritize the US run first and then spin EU instance - we'll include region tags in the logs
[09:10] Sara Gomez: also want to double-check: did you enable continuous batching or fixed time window batching? that's been a gotcha for us
[09:30] Liam Patel: we used a hybrid: continuous batching with a max latency window (30ms) and adaptive dropping for very long sequences. that's why batch sizes increased under normal loads. we can test fixed-window too if you want a deterministic comparison
[10:00] Tom Reeves: FYI our baseline used a 50ms window on their provider so might explain some differences
[10:18] Liam Patel: yep that aligns - smaller window trades lower latency for less throughput, which seems to match their higher p50 but worse throughput
[10:40] Sara Gomez: security question - how granular are audit logs if we go dedicated or private? need SSO integration and audit retention for 1 year
[11:00] Maya Chen: for Dedicated we expose admin-level audit logs, per-request tracing, and can push logs to your SIEM over a private peered connection. retention and SSO (SAML/SCIM) are configurable; we'll send the SOC2 summary and audit log spec after the call
[11:30] Priya Nair: perfect. on the performance side, can Redwood run the same benchmark with a slightly higher concurrency mix (16 clients) to see if p99 diverges? our prod will see spikes to 16+
[11:52] Liam Patel: yes we can run the 16-client and 32-client matrices over the weekend and share Monday, should give insight into autoscale behavior and tail under high contention
[12:20] Tom Reeves: regarding the 'rare cache misses' you mentioned - can you show us trace for one? we want to understand whether it's due to prefix variance or memory pressure
[12:40] Liam Patel: i'll include a couple trace samples in the logs; initial hypothesis is prefix mismatch on slightly different tokenization boundary which bypassed the cache, but we'll validate
[13:10] Sara Gomez: are there any vendor lock-in concerns if we adapt Redwood-specific optimizations like custom kernels or schema for KV cache?
[13:30] Maya Chen: our runtime uses standard model formats; KV cache format is documented. we can provide export hooks and migrating the cache is feasible. if you prefer non-proprietary paths we can lean on the open formats we support
[14:00] Priya Nair: small nit - the p99 number in your slide shows 420ms for tuned hosted and 980ms baseline, but the raw CSV had a few rows at ~1.8s, is that a recording artifact?
[14:22] Liam Patel: good catch - those were a couple of infra interruptions during one run (noisy neighbor on the instance we used for baseline sim). we removed those outliers for the summary slide but kept them in the raw logs with an outlier flag. i'll annotate them
[14:50] Maya Chen: ok, quick recap of the technical takeaway: Redwood hosted shows consistent mid-tail improvement with KV caching and adaptive batching; p99 still needs targeted work for very long generations - options are quantization, dedicated pools, and a canary with tuned autoscale thresholds
[15:18] Sara Gomez: sounds good. for decision criteria, we're focusing on p99 < 500ms for 95% of traffic and cost within 20% of baseline - can you help model that?
[15:38] Maya Chen: yes we'll run cost/perf sims with your traffic profile and share a proposal. Liam will include the GPU sizing and cost delta table
[16:05] Tom Reeves: timeline question: if we go dedicated, how long to provision? we have a compliance blackout starting Oct 10 so ideally before then
[16:28] Liam Patel: typical dedicated provisioning is 2-3 weeks after contract; we can prioritize and potentially shorten with a committed start date - we'll include options (fast vs standard) in the proposal
[16:50] Priya Nair: last thing - can we get a short postmortem on why baseline tail was so bad? even high level helps internal stakeholders
[17:10] Maya Chen: yes we'll prepare a one-pager explaining kernel scheduling, queue-time variance, and common tuning knobs. we'll include recommended mitigations and what Redwood changed in these runs
[17:40] Sara Gomez: thanks - that will help our procurement.
[18:00] Maya Chen: any other Qs?
[18:10] Priya Nair: none from me, thanks everyone
[18:20] Tom Reeves: i'm good
[18:28] Maya Chen: great, we'll circulate logs and the proposal. Liam, anything to add?
[18:36] Liam Patel: just that we'll run the 16/32 client matrices and include p95/p99 heatmaps by Monday, and attach the eval spreadsheet for quantization quality checks
[18:52] Maya Chen: perfect. recap of next steps: logs + csv + security pack by 2025-09-19, proposal and sizing by 2025-09-21, canary scheduling for 2025-09-26. thanks all!
[19:10] End of transcript (transcription contains some mis-hearings and small speaker label errors).
